e-21798.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
y''(x) + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = f(x), \qquad a \leq x \leq b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
\alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad 
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2
$$

where $P, Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ are real constants such that $(\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y \equiv 0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14077005/assets/f0ae121481e21c471d2e7b7eab072a2de438456dc76ac909db13b0262234fb80.png)

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y \equiv 0$ if and only if $\det(A) \neq 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting $\alpha_i = 0, \beta_i = 1, a = 0,$ and $b = \pi,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14077005/assets/f0cdf9d9e9f668853a863704ae8f72a6acd8842ffefff70a46e1d826f8b8a510.png)

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m = \pm 4\textrm i.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
y_1'(x) = -4\sin 4x, \qquad y_2'(x) = 4\cos 4x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \pi ) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|0\cdot 4-4\cdot 0| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\textrm{has infinitely many solutions}.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, our inhomogeneous BVP $\textrm{has infinitely many solutions or no solution}.$

Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem has a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=0,$ and $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-m-2 & =0 \\ (m-2)(m+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=2$ and $m=-1,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {e}^{2} & {e}^{-1}\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|{e}^{-1}-{e}^{2}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{e}-{e}^{2}| \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}-1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem has a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=0,$ and $b=1,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(0) & {y}_{2}(0) \\ {y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-m-2 & =0 \\ (m-2)(m+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=2$ and $m=-1,$ and so the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {e}^{2} & {e}^{-1}\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|{e}^{-1}-{e}^{2}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{e}-{e}^{2}| \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}-1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0$, our inhomogeneous BVP $\text{has a unique solution}.$

Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Specifically:

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & {y}_{2}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm \text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & cos\,(\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|0\cdot 0-1\cdot (-1)| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ our inhomogeneous BVP $\text{has at most one solution}.$

$$

- If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution $y≡0,$ then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & {y}_{2}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm \text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & cos\,(\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the corresponding homogeneous BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$
